3.0.s.en: (1) Concern for heavenly things and abandoning sin

3.0.0.en: Since you have risen with Christ, you must seek what befits your new nature, so direct your concern toward heavenly things and the things that qualify you for the eternal inheritance, and place your hope in the heavenly Kingdom, where Christ sits in the highest place.

3.1.0.en: Occupy your thoughts with the heavenly Kingdom and care for it and for everything that qualifies you for it, and do not care for the world and material things and everything that would bind you to the earth.

3.2.0.en: For when you were baptized you were buried with Christ, and so you died to sin and were freed from its dominion, and thereby you cut all the ties that bound you to the world.

3.2.1.en: The Greeks used to say of the dead person that he is hidden or concealed in the earth, and St. Paul uses the same expression, saying that after we died with Christ our life became hidden or concealed in Him. And just as the Gnostics claimed that the knowledge necessary for salvation is hidden in their books and concealed from the eyes of the world, we know that our life is hidden in Christ, our salvation and our hope, and concealed from the eyes of the world, who do not understand and do not want to understand the mystery of salvation.

3.3.0.en: "Shall appear": God will make Him appear at His Second Coming.

3.3.1.en: We now live in Christ, so when He comes in His glory at His Second Coming, we too will be glorified with Him.

3.3.2.en: Remember that you rose with Christ when you came up out of the water of Baptism and when you partake of His life-giving Body and Blood. So reject every sin into which you fall, because it is foreign to you, and seek in its place a life with God in prayers that lift you up to heaven.

3.4.0.en: The Apostle asks them to put to death the fleshly lusts that are committed by the members of the body, and here he lists five sins, which are:

3.4.1.en: "Fornication": which is the breaking of one of the Ten Commandments, "Thou shalt not commit adultery." There is also the figurative meaning of fornication, which is spiritual fornication, namely forsaking God and worshiping strange gods, as ancient paganism did in former times, and what is equivalent to it in the present times, the worship of money, position, fame ... etc.

3.4.2.en: "Uncleanness": which is the natural fruit of fornication and of sin in general, for sin defiles the heart, the mind, the body and the spirit.

3.4.3.en: "Inordinate affection": that is, unholy emotions, abnormal desires and the pursuit of pleasure.

3.4.4.en: "Evil concupiscence": a material desire against the commandments of God.

3.4.5.en: "Covetousness": the increasing desire to possess. Covetousness has been described as idolatry because it is attachment to material things, and if a person persists in it, he places all his hopes in them and offers them worship. By covetousness St. Paul may here mean covetousness in sexual matters, since he mentions it in connection with the sins of the flesh, such as a person coveting and lusting after a woman who is not lawful for him, whether another man's wife or any girl.

3.5.0.en: Because of these sins the wrath of God comes upon those who commit them, and the Apostle called them "children of disobedience" since they hold fast to disobedience to the end and so are ascribed to it. In addition, the sins of the flesh sometimes carry their punishment in themselves, such as the diseases associated with uncleanness, the latest of which is AIDS.

3.6.0.en: You Colossians were formerly among those who commit those sins, for the pagan Gentiles considered uncleanness a part of the rites of their worship, and you lived in an evil environment and so you walked according to its evil beliefs.

3.7.0.en: But now be freed from those vices and walk in the Spirit, and cast your former bitter sins far from you so that they do not cast you into outer darkness; the iniquities of the past and what has come from you are enough. St. Paul here points to five other sins, which are:

3.7.1.en: "Anger": which is the result of hatred, malice, and the loss of love and forbearance.

3.7.2.en: "Wrath": a violent expression of dissatisfaction with a certain attitude coming from others.

3.7.3.en: "Malice": the evil that holds within it the desire to harm others and to blame them.

3.7.4.en: "Blasphemy": cursing and slandering God, and its punishment in the Old Testament was death. "Filthy communication": improper words and silly sexual jokes.

3.8.0.en: St. Paul forbids lying, which is not telling the truth out of many motives, such as trying to obtain some undeserved advantages, or fear, or a sense of inferiority, or joking, and it brings a chain of dependent sins such as false swearing and then anger. It is not right for us to deceive others and lie to them, when what is right is that we must tell them the truth and not lies. So he calls them to leave the works that were characteristic of the fallen nature of man before renewal, especially since they have received the new nature, which grows and is renewed in the knowledge of God through spiritual striving until it becomes a true image of Him.

3.9.0.en: In this new nature you all become one in Christ, for the Lord Christ broke down the barriers between the Jews and the Gentiles. St. Paul mentioned certain classifications of people, namely: "Greek": who had a distinguished standing in society from the founding of the Greek Empire and even after the domination of the Roman Empire, and the Roman looked on one who did not speak Greek as a backward barbarian.

3.9.1.en: "Jew": one who prided himself on being a son of Abraham and had the Law and the promises, and the rest of the peoples were in his view unclean dogs.

3.9.2.en: "Circumcision": the Jews who are circumcised in their bodies in application of the Law.

3.9.3.en: "Uncircumcision": the peoples other than the Jews, who are not circumcised.

3.9.4.en: "Barbarian": one who does not speak Greek, who was looked upon with contempt.

3.9.5.en: "Scythian": one who lives north of the Black Sea; they were the harshest and most savage of the barbarians, so that the mere mention of their name stirred terror in souls.

3.9.6.en: "Bondman": one who had no human rights, and whose master had absolute freedom over him.

3.9.7.en: All of these, despite the great differences among them, if they accepted the faith, all became members of the one body of Christ, so that the whole body became the body of Christ, just as Christ dwelt in the hearts of all and so united them.

3.10.0.en: "Bowels of mercies": gentleness toward others springing from feelings of deep love.

3.10.1.en: "Meekness": the inward calm of the heart.

3.10.2.en: You Colossians, as those chosen by the Lord who loved you and redeemed you, adorn yourselves with the attributes and virtues of Christ and follow His example in compassion, humility, meekness and longsuffering.

3.11.0.en: Just as God bore with us and forgave us, and still does, so we must forgive our brethren if they wrong us. What helps us in this is our being adorned with the virtues mentioned in the previous verse. And our forgiveness of others is because God freely forgives us all our sins.

3.12.0.en: Above all the virtues mentioned, adorn yourselves with love, for it is the garment that gathers within it all the other virtues.

3.13.0.en: Hold fast to the peace that you obtained in the one body of Christ, and keep away from everything that disturbs your hearts, and give thanks to God for all His gifts.

3.14.0.en: Let the teachings of Christ dwell in you and abide in your hearts with a permanent abiding, and you must know them, so that you acquire all divine wisdom for dealing with others and for winning souls for the Kingdom by teaching them the foundation of the spiritual life and warning them to keep away from sin, using the Psalms, with their prayers of thanksgiving and praise that lift the soul to heaven, and the spiritual songs that stir in the soul reverence and spiritual joy, taking care for depth and spirituality so that your hearts touch the divine grace.

3.15.0.en: "In the name of the Lord Jesus": with the aim of pleasing Christ and for the glory of His blessed name. "By him": by Christ, by whose help and salvation we draw near to God and give Him thanks.

3.15.1.en: Let Christ be the aim of all your works and words, and give thanks to God for the salvation and the divine help.

3.15.2.en: Love is what moves every Christian, so look at God's love for you so that you give Him thanks and return love for love, and so overflow with mercy, tenderness and sacrifice for all who are around you.

3.16.s.en: (3) Advice to the members of the Christian family

3.16.0.en: The Apostle advises wives to submit to their husbands as they submit to the Lord. The wife offers submission to her husband as a sacrifice of love to Christ first, before it is to please her husband, and this suits the nature of the man, whose first demand is respect and appreciation, which moves him to meet the first demand of the woman, which is love, self-giving and kind words. Submission does not mean the man's domination but his leadership of the family, while decisions, after this submission, are made through understanding and love.

3.17.0.en: He also instructs men to love their wives as Christ loved the Church, for the bond between them is like the bond between Christ and the Church. Just as Christ gave Himself on the Cross for the Church, offering the highest feelings of love, so the husband must care for his wife and express his love for her every day with words of praise and support her in every need, and not use his leadership or his means to dominate her or be harsh toward her.

3.18.0.en: Children must obey their parents in all things, and the only condition for obeying parents is that it not conflict with the commandments of the Lord.

3.19.0.en: St. Paul advises fathers not to be severe in dealing with their children and not to increase their rebuking and punishing of them, lest they lose confidence in themselves and their personalities be shaken. They should not be asked for more than they are able, which helps them to carry out the commandment of obedience, so that he is pleased with them.

3.19.1.en: For your family to be truly Christian, you must feel the presence of Christ with you inside your home. Then you will care for the other party for the sake of Christ, who sees and hears everything you do and say. And you will care for your children with longsuffering, embracing them as Christ embraces your family.

3.20.0.en: "Your masters according to the flesh": that is, the earthly masters, because the spiritual Master, that is, God, is the most important, so we work to please Him in our dealings with our superiors.

3.20.1.en: "Eyeservice": pleasing the eyes of the masters while the heart is troubled by them or tries to neglect their orders. "Singleness of heart": purity and humility.

3.20.2.en: The Apostle instructs slaves to obey their masters who own them according to the laws by which society then operated. And he instructs them to be faithful in service, not in order that their masters may praise them but out of fear of the Lord.

3.21.0.en: Slaves must do the work required of them as if the work they do is offered to the Lord, doing it with sincerity and faithfulness of heart, knowing that the Lord will reward them for their faithfulness by making them sharers in the inheritance of eternal glory.

3.22.0.en: Those who treat others unjustly and are harsh to them, exploiting their authority in doing so, these will receive just retribution from God, who shows no partiality to anyone.

3.22.1.en: The fear of God protects you from many sins, and if you fall it makes you hasten to repentance and reassures your heart whatever the threats of others, and it moves you to love everyone, so that you receive divine tenderness and love. The Christian and society, then the conclusion

4.0.s.en: (1) Dealing with society and serving it

4.0.0.en: The Apostle asks the masters who own slaves to be gentle with them and not to wrong them, knowing that they are human beings like themselves, warning them that there is a higher Master for all, who is God, who judges for the wronged and takes vengeance on those who wrong them.

4.1.0.en: St. Paul gives the people of Colossae further spiritual advice, asking them to persevere in prayer, for it is the commandment of the Lord Christ to us (Lk 18:1), so we do not cease from prayer for any reason. Prayer must be with vigor and attention, giving thanks to God always, expressing our submission to the divine will and handing over all our affairs to Him.

4.2.0.en: At the beginning of his epistle Paul told them that he prays for them at all times, and at the end of the epistle here he asks for their prayers for him, that God may open before him the closed doors in preaching, remove the obstacles from the path of ministry, prepare minds to hear the word of God, and open hearts to faith when he speaks of the mystery of Christ, that is, the salvation that Christ accomplished for all and the opening of the door of faith to the Gentiles, for the preaching of which he was imprisoned.

4.3.0.en: "Them that are without": that is, the unbelievers.

4.3.1.en: "Redeeming the time": seizing the opportunity to work so that it is not wasted on what profits nothing. God instructs us to be wise as serpents (Mt 10:16). Wisdom requires walking uprightly, carefully and blamelessly, especially in our dealings with unbelievers, so that our mixing with them is within limits, for they watch our conduct, on the basis of which they glorify our Father who is in heaven or blaspheme Him because of us.

4.4.0.en: When grace dwells in our hearts, our speech is with love, gentleness and humility, and so it imparts grace to the hearers. Just as salt is put in food so that the one who eats may taste it, so let your speech be marked by meekness and gentleness so that it may be easily accepted by others.

4.4.1.en: Seek God before every word or action, and He will guide you by His wisdom to all that is good, and will cover your weakness and even glorify you in the eyes of others, so that they see in you the love of God and His righteousness and love Him because of you.

4.5.s.en: (2) Greetings from Paul and his disciples

4.5.0.en: In this passage St. Paul sends them the greetings of ten of his disciples who work with him in the Lord's vineyard, namely:

4.5.1.en: Tychicus, Onesimus, Aristarchus, Mark, Jesus who is called Justus, Epaphras, Luke, Demas, Nymphas, Archippus.

4.5.2.en: He begins by praising Tychicus and calls him a beloved brother, raising him to be on an equal footing with himself, although he is his disciple, giving us a lesson in humility. Tychicus was a faithful servant who carried out his ministry with diligence and perseverance. He will make known to the people of Colossae the news of Paul so that they may be reassured about him.

4.6.0.en: St. Paul also sent his disciple Tychicus to Colossae to learn their news and to encourage them in the spiritual life.

4.7.0.en: Paul sent with Tychicus another disciple, Onesimus, who is a slave of Philemon, who lived in the city of Colossae, which is why Paul says of him, "who is one of you." He will undertake with Tychicus to inform the people of Colossae of what is happening in Rome, where St. Paul is imprisoned.

4.8.0.en: He conveys to them the greeting of Aristarchus, who is imprisoned with him, and also the greeting of St. Mark, the nephew of Barnabas and Paul's companion on many journeys. St. Paul had earlier sent recommendations on his behalf to the churches of Asia Minor, so that they would receive him as an apostle of Christ, and he repeats this recommendation here.

4.9.0.en: "Jesus, which is called Justus": one of Paul's disciples, who also sends his greeting to the people of Colossae.

4.9.1.en: "Who are of the circumcision": he means Aristarchus, Mark and Justus, because they are of Jewish origin and circumcised as the Law requires.

4.9.2.en: "Only": the disciples of Paul mentioned here are the ones who were helping him in preaching at that time in Rome.

4.9.3.en: "Have been a comfort unto me": their sharing with Paul in the ministry comforted and strengthened him in the midst of the affliction of prison. This shows the humility of Paul, who declares his need for comfort and encouragement from his children. Those whom Paul mentioned work with him to spread the word of the Gospel, and they became a comfort to him in the time of affliction.

4.9.4.en: Be strong and face yourself to know your spiritual, psychological and material needs, so that you ask for them from God and thank everyone who provides them to you, however much younger or lesser than you he may be, for this teaches you humility and encourages and gladdens the others whom you thank.

4.10.0.en: He sends them the greetings of Epaphras, who is from among the Gentiles, a disciple of Paul and the founder of the three churches of Phrygia (Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis), and he called him a servant of Christ, for he is one of the heroes of the faith. Epaphras was a beautiful example of perseverance in prayer, and he strove in it so that the Lord might grant grace to the believers, that they might stand firm in the faith and not be affected by innovations and heresies, doing the will of God.

4.11.0.en: St. Paul noticed the fervent prayer of Epaphras, so he bore witness to his zeal for the salvation of his children in the faith and his care for them and for the churches he founded in Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis.

4.12.0.en: He sends them the greeting of Luke the physician, who combined the two virtues of love and mercy, which he acquired from his original profession as a physician. Before his faith he treated only bodies, but after his faith he became a physician of souls and bodies.

4.12.1.en: "Demas": the only one of the ten disciples who did not receive a single word of praise from his teacher Paul, perhaps because he sensed the inclination of his heart toward the present world. And this indeed happened, and it is mentioned in (2 Tim 4:10) where he said of him, "Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world."

4.13.0.en: Paul sends his greeting to the brethren in Laodicea, which is very near to Colossae, since with it and the neighboring city of Hierapolis it forms the region of preaching of Epaphras, the disciple of Paul.

4.13.1.en: "Nymphas": one of the well-to-do Laodicean brethren, who opened his house as a church for the worship of the believers.

4.14.0.en: Here Paul asks the people of Colossae to send this epistle after reading it to Laodicea to be read there, and that they ask Laodicea for the epistle that Paul had sent to them so that it may be read among them also. The commentators agree that the epistle meant is the Epistle to the Ephesians, because it was addressed to all the churches neighboring Ephesus and not only to the church of Ephesus.

4.15.0.en: "Archippus": a servant in the church of Colossae, perhaps an assistant to Epaphras, who led the church during his absence in Rome when he visited Paul. Some think that he was the son of Philemon because he is mentioned in the epistle sent to him.

4.15.1.en: Paul's charge to Archippus is directed to every servant, and it is that the ministry he carries out is in Christ, so he should care for it and complete it by the power of God and for His sake, so that a servant does not begin a ministry and then become negligent in it or in any of its details.

4.16.0.en: The heretics used to forge the epistles of St. Paul, so he would put a mark on his epistle by writing this last phrase in addition to his signature on the epistle.

4.16.1.en: "Remember my bonds": the Apostle gives them an example of faithfulness and self-giving sacrifice, so that they do not weaken before persecutions, but remember the labors of their teacher, so that their souls are filled with readiness for self-giving and sacrifice in his likeness. St. Paul ends his epistle by asking grace for them, which suffices them and enriches them.

4.16.2.en: Paul wrote this epistle from within his prison in Rome, and he dictated it to his two disciples Tychicus and Onesimus.
